body.heading: The same both ways
paragraphs: A palindrome reads identically forwards and backwards. Small ones hide in everyday speech: noon, level, madam, kayak, racecar. Say 'racecar' slowly in reverse and you will hear the trick — the letters are arranged like a reflection in a mirror.

Names can be palindromes too: Hannah, Ava and Otto all read the same both ways. Dates sometimes join in — 02/02/2020 was a palindromic date in both day-first and month-first formats, a small gift to calendar watchers.

body.heading: Whole sentences that loop
paragraphs: With spaces and punctuation ignored, entire sentences can loop. 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?' reads the same backwards. The most famous example celebrates a feat of engineering: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama!'

Building a sentence palindrome is genuinely hard, because every letter you add at the front demands a matching letter at the back. Short ones are a good start — try to make a three-word loop about an animal before attempting a masterpiece.

body.heading: Hunt for your own
paragraphs: Go hunting: check the names in your family, your street, your favourite foods and games. Radar, civic, rotor, stats and solos are all hiding in plain sight. Words ending in the same letter they start with are promising candidates.
Keep a list on your phone. Palindromes are the kind of small discovery that improves a whole afternoon — and the next one you find will feel like it was waiting for you.

takeaway: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards — and once you start looking, they hide in names, places and everyday words.
